analysis.one_liner: Caps ride-hail platforms' cut of fares at 25% and forces app-based work platforms to disclose pay, pricing, and algorithm details.
analysis.headline: A bill to force app-work platforms to disclose their pay and pricing algorithms and cap ride-hail companies' cut of fares at 25% was introduced on December 11, 2025, with 14 cosponsors, and has not advanced past its first House committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets companies like Uber, Lyft, and DoorDash that manage workers through apps. It would cap the share of a ride fare the company keeps at 25% — meaning drivers would keep at least 75% of what riders pay. It would also require these platforms to tell workers how algorithms set their pay and assignments, give itemized receipts showing what the customer paid versus what the worker got, ban paying different workers different rates for the same work based on personal data, and let workers, unions, and consumers sue with damages of up to $25,000 or more per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: App-based workers — especially the more than a million ride-hail drivers, who are disproportionately people of color and often earn less than minimum wage after expenses — gain a guaranteed 75% share of fares, itemized pay receipts, and notice of how algorithms decide their pay and work. Consumers gain disclosure of what the platform takes from each fare.

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps the 'take rate' — the share of a ride fare the platform keeps — at 25%, so drivers keep at least 75% of what riders pay, excluding tips [S2].
Platforms must give workers itemized receipts after every job and weekly pay statements showing what the customer paid, what the worker received, and the take rate [S2].

Platforms must disclose to workers how electronic monitoring and automated systems set pay, assignments, and prices, and cannot use individualized worker data to pay different workers different rates for the same work [S2].

The bill voids forced arbitration agreements and non-disclosure clauses between workers and platforms, and protects workers from retaliation — including account deactivation — for asserting these rights, with statutory damages of $5,000 to $25,000 per violation and Department of Labor penalties of up to $100,000 for willful violations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ride-hail and delivery platform companies and their investors bear the cost: reduced share of fares, detailed disclosure and recordkeeping, litigation exposure with stiff statutory damages, and limits on the algorithmic pricing and worker-surveillance tools that generate their margins. Some of that cost may be passed to consumers through higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Uber, Lyft, DoorDash and their investors

drawbacks.text: A 25% take-rate cap could push companies to raise rider prices, cut bonuses, or reduce driver recruitment in thin markets, so some of the cost may land on consumers [S2].

The compliance burden — notices, receipts, quarterly reporting, four-year data retention, and civil penalties starting at $20,000–$25,000 per violation — falls hardest on smaller platforms, and Section 12 sends all legal challenges to the rules to a single court (the D.C. district court) with a deferential standard of review, limiting workers' ability to challenge weak regulations [S2].

The bill does not resolve the underlying question of whether app workers are employees or independent contractors; it adds transparency and pay rules without guaranteeing minimum wage, overtime, or benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and large for workers in the least transparent corner of the labor market: drivers who currently see up to 60% of a fare kept by the platform would be guaranteed at least 75%. The main costs are price increases for riders, compliance costs that squeeze smaller platforms, and litigation designed to be aggressively punitive toward platform companies. The disclosure and pay-statement requirements are hard to argue against on the merits; the take-rate cap and sweeping damages are where reasonable people split.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2025, and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor action; it has not yet come up for any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-WA) introduced the bill with nine original cosponsors on December 11, 2025 [S1][S2].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Workforce on the day of introduction, and no further action appears in the record [S4].
Fourteen members have cosponsored the bill — 13 Democrats and 1 Republican [S3].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote has been scheduled or taken [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, no one has won or lost — the bill is simply sitting in committee. To the extent the status quo persists, app-based platform companies continue operating under current pay practices and take rates, while the million-plus workers the bill targets keep the pay and transparency arrangements they have today.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 cosponsors; wrote it around a 25% ride-hail take-rate cap and full algorithmic pay disclosure.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors (13 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including original cosponsors Reps. Norcross, Omar, Takano, Pocan, Tlaib, and Norton [S2][S3].

sides.party_line_note: All 13 Democratic cosponsors are joined by a single Republican; no Republican opposition has been recorded because the bill has not yet reached any vote, and with Republicans holding the House majority, one cross-party cosponsor is not enough to move it.

industries.note: The 25% take-rate cap directly limits the share of each fare these companies keep — findings in the bill document rates rising toward 60% of the fare. Their profit model of setting rider prices independently of driver pay is the bill's central target [S2].

industries.industry: Delivery and gig-work platforms (DoorDash, Instacart, Amazon Flex)
industries.note: They are not subject to the take-rate cap (which covers on-demand transportation only) but face the full disclosure regime: pay receipts, algorithm transparency, bans on individualized pay-setting, data limits, voided arbitration clauses, and litigation exposure [S2].

Vendors that supply monitoring and decision software face joint and several liability with platforms for data violations, restrictions on what data can be collected and inferred, and a ban on selling worker data [S2].
Consumers gain disclosure of what the platform takes from each fare, but companies may raise prices to offset the take-rate cap and compliance costs [S2].

analysis.trajectory: Most bills introduced in the House die in committee without a hearing, and this one was just referred to the Education and Workforce Committee, which is chaired by the opposing party with no announced plans for it. With only one Republican cosponsor and no committee action weeks after introduction, the realistic path is that the bill stalls out unless it gains substantially more bipartisan support or Democrats take the House in 2026 and its sponsor gains a committee gavel or leadership interest.
